opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because trust isn't something you get all at once. It's built up through a lot of small interactions, kind of like how you'd build trust with a new colleague.

The way I see it, there's a progression. At first you're collaborating really closely. You're in the loop on every step, the model is showing its work, and you're editing what it produces. That's where things like Canvas-style interfaces matter, because they make the model's reasoning and output something you can see, inspect, and change. You're co-creating rather than handing something off and hoping for the best.

Over time, as the model keeps doing well on the kinds of tasks you care about, you start loosening your grip. You stop checking every line. You let it do a first draft of the whole thing, then maybe a whole workflow. Delegation comes out of that track record. People will hand over more autonomy when they've seen the model be reliable, and especially when they've seen it be honest about what it doesn't know.

That last part is really important to me. A big piece of trust is calibration: the model asking clarifying questions when something is ambiguous, saying "I'm not sure" instead of confidently making things up, and checking in at the right moments without being annoying. If an agent interrupts you constantly, you won't want to delegate to it. If it never checks in, you can't trust it with anything high-stakes. Getting that balance right is a research problem and a product design problem at the same time.

So from the modeling side, I think a lot about what behaviors we're actually teaching through post-training. Not just "can it complete the task," but "does it collaborate well, does it know when to defer, can it explain what it did afterward so you can verify it?" And on the interface side, it's about giving people the right affordances to supervise. Things like reviewing a plan before execution, seeing a summary of what changed, and being able to easily undo.

Ideally, collaboration is the training ground for delegation. The better the collaborative experience, the faster people can build the intuition and confidence to say, "okay, go handle this for me." And I think that's how we get to agents that people actually rely on day to day, rather than ones that are impressive in a demo but that nobody trusts with real work.

r001.rationale: The response says trust builds through repeated small interactions and calls collaboration the training ground for delegation, explicitly linking consistent collaboration to greater trust.

r002.rationale: The response discusses building intuition and confidence through collaboration, but does not state that collaboration reveals implicit user preferences that enable fuller delegation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that trust with agents gets built the same way it gets built with a new colleague, which is incrementally and through shared context, not through a leap of faith.

When I think about the arc, it starts with collaboration that's very tight-loop. You're working alongside the model, you see every step, you correct it in real time. That phase matters not because the model can't do more, but because you're learning its judgment. You start to notice where it's reliably good, where it over-reaches, where it quietly narrows the task to the easy part. And the model, if the system is designed well, is learning you too: your taste, your constraints, what "done" means in your context.

Then delegation becomes possible when a few things are true. First, the agent has to be legible. I should be able to understand what it did and why without rerunning everything myself. That means good summaries, honest reporting when something failed or got skipped, and not dressing up partial work as complete. Second, there has to be a sense of reversibility. I'm much more willing to hand off a task if I know the agent will pause before the irreversible actions and run freely on the reversible ones. That asymmetry is really the whole thing. Third, the agent needs the right instinct about when to ask versus when to decide. If it asks about everything, it's not delegation, it's babysitting. If it never asks, you can't trust it with anything that matters.

I also think memory and continuity are underrated here. A lot of what makes a human colleague trustworthy is that they remember the last time you said "don't do it that way." If an agent starts every session from zero, you're perpetually stuck in the supervision phase. Once it can carry forward your preferences and the reasons behind them, the trust compounds.

And honestly, the last piece is that trust should be scoped, not global. I might fully delegate code review triage to an agent and still want to be in the loop on anything customer-facing. Good systems let you grant trust task by task, and good agents don't treat approval in one context as license in another. That's where I think the field should be building: not toward "do you trust the agent," but toward "what exactly have you trusted it with, and does it know the boundary as well as you do."

r001.rationale: The response says trust builds incrementally through close collaboration, where the user observes and corrects the agent over time.

r002.rationale: It says the agent learns the user's taste, constraints, and definition of “done,” and that carrying those preferences forward makes delegation possible.

astra-6.text:
I think trust has to be built gradually. You start with a small, well-defined task where you can inspect the result and understand what the agent did. Then, as it demonstrates that it can handle those tasks reliably, you give it more responsibility.

A big part of that is how it handles uncertainty. Does it ask for clarification when it needs to? Does it tell you when something went wrong? An agent that confidently says everything is done when it’s actually stuck is very hard to delegate to.

So I think collaboration is the process through which you learn what you can trust it with. You develop a sense of its strengths and limitations, and ideally it also gets better at understanding your preferences. Over time, you move from supervising every step to agreeing on an outcome and checking in at the points where your judgment matters.

r001.rationale: It says collaboration is how you learn what to trust the agent with, building responsibility gradually as it proves reliable.

r002.rationale: It says the agent ideally gets better at understanding your preferences, supporting a shift toward delegating based on agreed outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think trust has to build gradually through collaboration. You start with a small task where you can inspect the result and understand what the agent did. As it demonstrates that it understands your intent, you can give it more responsibility.

A big part of that is how it handles uncertainty. Does it ask a useful question when something is ambiguous? Does it tell you when it’s stuck? Can you correct it and see that correction reflected in what it does next? Those interactions help you calibrate how much you can delegate.

So I’d want the agent to make its work easy to review and give you opportunities to intervene. Over time, you can move from checking every step to checking the outcome, because you’ve developed a shared understanding of what good work looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says trust builds gradually through collaboration, starting with small tasks and increasing responsibility as the agent demonstrates understanding.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning the user's intent and developing a shared understanding of good work, but does not clearly state that collaboration reveals implicit user preferences.
